source.title: Scaling, but not instruction tuning, increases large language models’ alignment with language processing in the human brain
source.authors: Changjiang Gao; Zhengwu Ma; Jia-Jun Chen; Ping Li; Shujian Huang; Jixing Li

record.file_problem: The supplied text is a complete article. Its header identifies it as a Nature Computational Science article, although the supplied ID and venue identify a bioRxiv record.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures next-word prediction loss on experimental text across existing language models of different sizes, rather than fitting scaling laws using controlled training sweeps.
record.gate_note: The study reports mean next-word prediction loss on 148 test-stimulus sentences. It does not fit a power law or test extrapolation, compute-optimal allocations, architecture effects, or scaling of held-out pretraining loss across controlled runs. Brain- and eye-alignment analyses and attention-pattern analyses concern different outcomes; they are not recorded as claim-version rows.
record.test_reason: The study is about how well model attention aligns with human eye movements and fMRI. Next-word-prediction (NWP) loss on 148 reading-stimulus sentences is only a preliminary check of existing models. The models come from families with different training data (GPT-2, LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral). There is no controlled sweep, no held-out pretraining loss, no power-law fit and no data or compute axis. Its one loss result, that loss falls with size, cannot show whether V1's power-law form holds. The scaling laws (Kaplan et al.) are cited as motivation. The paper's 'scaling law' result concerns brain and eye alignment, a different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. On their stimuli, base-model NWP loss decreased with size and instruction-tuned models did not improve NWP. The main conclusion is that scaling, not instruction tuning, improves the match of attention with eye-movement and fMRI patterns. The authors also report this held in a Chinese listening dataset with LLaMA3 8B and 70B models.
record.recipe_differences: Uses pre-existing model families and measures next-word prediction loss on experimental reading stimuli; it does not train a controlled model-size, token-count, or compute sweep or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported next-word prediction result differs between base and instruction-tuned models. The paper does not report sensitivity of a scaling-law fit to fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Attention-based alignment with regressive eye saccades and with fMRI responses rises with log parameter count from 774M to 65B. The authors call this 'a clear scaling law of model–behavior alignment'. Instruction tuning does not change it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model–brain and model–behaviour alignment of LLM attention improves with parameter scale but not with instruction tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: On the 148 reading stimuli, mean NWP loss falls with size for base models. Instruction-tuned models show no NWP loss improvement over their base models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss on small out-of-domain text sets decreases with base-model size across model families, and instruction tuning does not lower it.

record.problems: The next-word prediction result is on 148 stimulus sentences, and the supplied text does not give numeric loss values for individual models. Model families differ in training data and other setup details; there is no controlled sweep or power-law fit.
record.rows_left_out: Brain/eye alignment, attention divergence, and trivial-pattern results are not measurements of the claim versions recorded here. Other cited scaling-law results are not the study's own results.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss, power-law form, and the token and compute axes were not tested. Only a monotonic trend in stimulus-set NWP loss across heterogeneous model families is reported.

record.verdict_notes: No verdicts are given because no claim version is tested. The study's 'scaling law' refers to brain-encoding performance. The NWP comparison is a z-scored, per-sentence t-test across model pairs, not a loss-scaling fit.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures next-word prediction loss on its reading-stimulus text, but does not fit or test a power-law functional form, vary training tokens or compute, or establish which quantities are non-bottlenecks.
No predictions from fits on small runs are tested against larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between model parameters and tokens is tested.
The study does not compare architecture variations at fixed parameter count.
The study does not test other modalities or training regimes as cases of the claimed loss scaling law.
The study does not test downstream task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not compare scaling-law fits, exponents, or compute-optimal allocations across fitting choices.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Base models on the Reading Brain test stimuli
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that next-word prediction loss trends downward as base-model size increases (r1–r8); the study does not establish a power-law fit.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Instruction-tuned models on the same test stimuli
reader_labels.reason: The authors report no next-word prediction improvement for the fine-tuned models (r9–r14); the measurement is also limited to one small set of test text and does not fit a scaling function.
